fetched_contents.text: How to treat the common cold at home: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia Colds are very common. A visit with your health care provider is often not needed, and most colds get better in about a week. Some symptoms, such as runny nose and cough can last 14 days or longer. A type of germ called a virus causes most colds. There are many types of viruses that can cause a cold. Depending on what virus you have, your symptoms may vary. Common symptoms of a cold include: * Fever (100°F [37.7°C] or higher) and chills * Headache, sore muscles, and fatigue * Cough * Nasal symptoms, such as stuffiness, runny nose, yellow or green mucus, and sneezing * Sore throat Mild symptoms of COVID-19 may be similar to those of the common cold. Always check with your provider if you are at risk for COVID-19. Treating your symptoms will not make your cold go away, but it will help you feel better. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) and ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) help lower fever and relieve muscle aches. Aspirin can also treat a cold, but it may have potential serious side effects, such as stomach bleeding. So it's best to avoid using aspirin. Aspirin should never be used in children and teens due to the risk of Reye syndrome. When taking over-the-counter (OTC) pain relievers: * Check the label for the proper dose. * Contact your provider if you need to take these medicines more than 4 times per day or for more than 2 or 3 days. OTC cold and cough medicines may help ease symptoms in adults and older children. * Do not give OTC cough and cold medicine to children under age 4, as they can have serious side effects. * For children ages 4 to 6 years, contact your provider before giving your child OTC cold medicine. * If you take prescription medicines for another health problem, ask your provider which OTC cold medicines are safe for you. Many OTC multi-symptom cough and cold medicines use more than one medicine. * Instead of buying OTC remedies with multiple medicines, treat each symptom individually. That way you know how much you are taking of each medicine. * If you do opt for these medicines, be sure to read the labels carefully to make sure you do not take too much of any one medicine. To treat individual symptoms: * A nasal decongestant can help relieve stuffiness and a runny nose. * Throat lozenges or sprays can help ease a sore throat. * Coughing is your body's way of getting mucus out of your lungs. So only use cough medicines if needed. * A cough suppressant can help if your cough keeps you from getting enough rest or sleeping at night. * If you are coughing up thick mucus, a cough expectorant may help. It thins mucus so it's easier to cough it up. Here are other things you can do to help relieve a cold: * Drink plenty of water and other fluids without caffeine. You lose a lot of fluid from coughing and blowing your nose, and this will help you stay hydrated. * Gargle with warm salt water to help relieve a sore throat. * Prop yourself up with pillows at night to help relieve your cough so you can sleep. * A humidifier may help ease symptoms. Follow all instructions for cleaning the machine. * Breathe in steam by taking a hot shower, or putting your head under a towel and over a bowl of hot water. * Take time to rest and get plenty of sleep. * Stay away from secondhand smoke. Wheezing can be a common symptom of a cold if you have asthma. * Use your rescue inhaler as prescribed if you are wheezing. * See your provider immediately if it becomes hard to breathe. Do not ask your provider for antibiotics to treat a common cold. Keep in mind that antibiotics kill bacteria. They will not treat a common cold, which is caused by a virus. Many home remedies are popular treatments for the common cold. These include vitamin C, zinc supplements, and echinacea. Although not proven to be helpful, most home remedies are safe for most people. * Some remedies may cause side effects or allergic reactions. * Certain remedies may change the way other medicines work. * Contact your provider before trying any herbs and supplements. Wash your hands often. This is the best way to stop the spread of germs. To wash your hands correctly: * Rub soap onto wet hands for 20 seconds. Make sure to get under your fingernails. Dry your hands with a clean towel or air dryer and turn the faucet off with a towel. * You can also use alcohol-based hand sanitizers with at least 60% alcohol. Use a dime sized amount and rub all over your hands until they are dry. To further prevent colds: * Stay home when you are sick. * Cough or sneeze into a tissue or into the crook of your elbow and not into the air. Try treating your cold at home first. fetched_contents.text: When Should I See a Doctor for a Cold or Flu? You already know that a scratchy throat, annoying cough, and lots of sneezing are part of the game. You can also probably count on a stuffy nose and some aches and pains. But when is it time to put down the chicken soup and get some advice from a pro? Take stock of your symptoms and see if they fit into one of these patterns: You have trouble breathing or chest pain. Your cold or flu shouldn't make you short of breath or cause your chest to hurt. If that's happening to you, it could be a sign of a more serious problem, such as heart disease, asthma, or pneumonia. Call your doctor or go to the emergency room. Your fever doesn't get better. If it won't go away it might mean you've got another infection in your body that needs treatment. Generally, a fever for an adult is a temperature over 100.4 degrees F. You can't keep anything down. Your body needs fluids to work right. If you can't drink anything without vomiting, you may need to go to your doctor's office or the hospital to get fluids through an IV. It hurts to swallow. That's not normal. Although a sore throat can make it hurt a little to swallow, severe pain can be a sign of an infection or injury that needs to be treated by a doctor. You can't get rid of your cough. If it doesn't go away, it's likely due to postnasal drip -- mucus that moves from your nose into your throat. It can be treated with antihistamines. But it could also be related to asthma or GERD (gastroesophageal reflux disease). Your doctor can tell you what to do for it. A lasting, severe cough is also the main symptom of whooping cough, a disease that's become more common in many parts of the U.S. So, if you've been hacking away for more than 2-3 weeks, your doctor may give you a test to see if you've got it. Your congestion and headache won't go away. Colds and allergies that block your nose with mucus can lead to a sinus infection. If your cold medicine doesn't give you relief, see your doctor for more treatment.

fetched_contents.title: Decongestants and Antihistamines for a Cold
fetched_contents.text: Decongestants and Antihistamines for a Cold Are you all stuffed up and sneezing away because of a cold? Decongestants and antihistamines can help. They come in different forms and are often mixed into combination drugs that you can buy without a prescription. It pays to do a little homework to make sure you're picking the right medicine for your symptoms. A decongestant is a medication that helps ease nasal congestion, which happens when something irritates the lining of your nose. This can result from a cold, the flu, or allergies, for example. A nasal decongestant helps reduce swelling in the blood vessels in your nose. This can ease the feeling of pressure in your nose, clear up a stuffy or runny nose, and help you breathe better. While nasal decongestants can clear up symptoms such as a runny nose, they don’t address the cause of your symptoms. If a cold is causing your symptoms, for example, a decongestant won’t cure or get rid of your cold, but it can provide some relief while the cold runs its course. The common cold usually lasts 7-10 days. Decongestants are available as pills, liquids, nasal sprays, and nasal drops. How to find a good decongestant Two common decongestants are pseudoephedrine and phenylephrine. However, in November 2024, the FDA proposed removing oral phenylephrine as an active ingredient in over-the-counter (OTC) nasal decongestant drug products. The FDA reviewed data and found that oral phenylephrine is not effective as a nasal decongestant, but it is safe. This means that oral drugs for nasal congestion that contain phenylephrine are safe to take, but they may not work. The FDA may issue a final order on what drugs can be marketed. The FDA’s proposed order doesn’t apply to nasal sprays that contain phenylephrine. Those are still considered effective. Many decongestant medications contain multiple ingredients, such as phenylephrine or pseudoephedrine, along with ingredients like dextromethorphan (to relieve cough) or acetaminophen (to relieve pain). According to the FDA, the presence of phenylephrine in a medication doesn’t affect how the other ingredients work. You may prefer decongestants in different formulations, like nasal sprays rather than pills. If you’re looking for a pill or liquid, you might choose a medication that contains an active ingredient that’s not phenylephrine. If you’re using a decongestant nasal spray, you shouldn’t use it for more than three or four days, because it can make your symptoms worse. Along with OTC nasal decongestants, some decongestant drugs are available only with a prescription. An antihistamine is a type of medication that is used to relieve or prevent allergy symptoms such as runny nose, sneezing, and watery eyes. Antihistamines work by blocking histamine — a chemical your body makes that can cause nasal congestion and other symptoms. However, some research has found that antihistamines don’t work well to treat the common cold. Many different antihistamines exist. They include: * First-generation antihistamines, such as brompheniramine and chlorpheniramine * Second-generation antihistamines, such as fexofenadine and loratadine First-generation antihistamines are known to cause drowsiness, but second-generation ones are not. These also help prevent losing too much fluid, called dehydration. Don't drink alcohol, coffee and sodas with caffeine. They can make dehydration worse. * Rest. You can use saline nasal sprays in older children. Relieve pain Adults can take acetaminophen (Tylenol, others), ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin IB, others) or aspirin. For treatment of fever or pain, consider giving your child infants' or children's versions of medicines available without a prescription. Examples are acetaminophen (Tylenol, others) or ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin, others). These can be used as a safer alternative to aspirin. Try cold and cough medicines For adults and children age 5 and older, decongestants, antihistamines and pain relievers available without a prescription might ease some symptoms. Daily things to do for symptom management

The evidence points to a consistent self-care pattern for a runny nose and mild cough without fever: rest, hydration, safe symptom-specific actions, and careful symptom monitoring at home. The most supported daily habits are drinking plenty of fluids without caffeine, rest, and using symptom-specific remedies only when needed [N1-F1][N4-R3][N5-F4]. MedlinePlus emphasizes that most cold symptoms do not require specific treatment and that symptom management is the main goal [N1-R3][N1-F1]. It also notes that fluids help stay hydrated, especially since coughing and blowing the nose can cause fluid loss [N1-F1].

For runny nose, the evidence supports saline nasal drops/sprays and nasal decongestants as daily options, but only with caution. MedlinePlus says nasal decongestants can help relieve stuffiness and a runny nose, while Mayo Clinic recommends saline nasal drops and sprays without a prescription for stuffiness [N1-F1][N4-R3][N5-F4]. Vicks lists nasal sprays among OTC solutions for runny nose and nasal congestion [N3-R5]. However, the evidence also says decongestants are not a cure and should not be used for more than 3–4 days if they are nasal sprays [N3-F3]. That means daily use should be limited and monitored.

For cough, the evidence supports using cough suppressants only if the cough keeps you from resting or sleeping, and expectorants if coughing up thick mucus [N1-F1][N5-F4]. Mayo Clinic also mentions cough medicine, but notes that cough suppressants should be used selectively because cough is a natural defense mechanism [N4-R4]. MedlinePlus adds that cough medicines are for adults and older children, and not for children under age 4 [N1-F1]. The broader safe daily habit is therefore to treat cough only as needed and not overuse OTC products.

Environmental and sleep habits are also central. MedlinePlus and Mayo Clinic both recommend staying away from secondhand smoke, using a humidifier or cool-mist vaporizer, and sleeping with pillows to relieve cough [N1-F1][N4-R4][N5-F4]. Mayo Clinic also specifically mentions adjusting room temperature and humidity [N4-R3]. The evidence supports a humidifier as helpful for breathing comfort and for people with allergies, asthma, or frequent cough [N4-R2][N4-R5]. This is a daily habit that can ease symptoms while staying at home.

Safe remedies or actions to take every day include gargling with warm salt water for a sore throat, drinking warm liquids, and using throat lozenges or sprays [N1-F1][N4-R4][N5-F4]. MedlinePlus also recommends using a humidifier, propelling up with pillows, and avoiding alcohol and tobacco smoke [N1-F1]. These are all supported daily actions, but the evidence is strongest for the basics: fluids, rest, avoiding irritants, and symptom-specific remedies only when needed.

Monitoring symptoms while staying at home is explicitly part of the guidance. MedlinePlus says symptoms may last 14 days or longer and that you should contact a provider if symptoms get worse or do not improve after 10 days [N1-F1]. It also says to seek care immediately if it becomes hard to breathe [N1-F1]. Mayo Clinic’s symptom-monitoring guidance is less explicit in the excerpt provided, but the broader evidence still supports tracking worsening symptoms, persistent cough, or signs that daily self-care is no longer enough [N2-F2][N4-F2]. The practical monitoring rule is therefore to note how long symptoms last and whether they improve, stay the same, or get worse [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Overall, the daily things to do are:
1. Drink plenty of water and other fluids without caffeine [N1-F1][N4-R3][N5-F4].
2. Rest and get plenty of sleep [N1-F1][N4-R3].
3. Use saline nasal drops/sprays or nasal decongestants as needed, but limit nasal sprays to 3–4 days [N1-F1][N4-R3][N3-F3].
4. Use cough suppressants only if needed and expectorants if coughing up thick mucus [N1-F1][N5-F4].
5. Stay away from secondhand smoke, use a humidifier or cool-mist vaporizer, and sleep with pillows to relieve cough [N1-F1][N4-R4][N4-R2][N4-R5].

These actions are supported by the evidence as safe, symptom-focused daily habits.

Daily things to avoid or be cautious about

The evidence clearly identifies several common mistakes and harmful behaviors to avoid. First, alcohol and tobacco smoke should be avoided, as they can worsen symptoms [N1-F1][N4-R4]. MedlinePlus also says to avoid alcohol and tobacco smoke [N1-F1], and Mayo Clinic similarly recommends avoiding tobacco smoke [N4-R4]. This is a strong daily caution.

Second, overuse or misuse of OTC medicines is a major red flag. MedlinePlus says to avoid taking OTC medicines more than 4 times per day or for more than 2 or 3 days [N1-F1]. It also warns that taking too much of any one medicine can be dangerous [N1-F1]. Mayo Clinic explicitly says to read labels carefully and not take too much of any medicine [N5-F4]. The evidence also says that some cold remedies have mixed ingredients and using too much can cause serious damage [N5-F4]. That means people should be cautious about combining medicines or relying on multi-symptom products without understanding the contents.

Third, certain treatments should not be used for children. MedlinePlus says OTC cough and cold medicine should not be given to children under age 4, and for children ages 4–6, contact a provider before giving OTC cold medicine [N1-F1]. CDC and other sources echo this caution: OTC cold medicines are not recommended for children younger than 6 years old and can result in serious side effects [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The evidence also says over-the-counter cough and cold medications are not effective in treating children with the common cold and might cause serious side effects, including death [N6-R3]. This is a key daily caution for caregivers.

Fourth, specific treatments should be stopped or avoided if they are not clearly helpful. The evidence says nasal decongestants are not a cure and should not be used for more than 3–4 days if they are nasal sprays [N3-F3]. It also says antihistamines are not very effective for treating the common cold and most experts say histamine is not the major cause of a runny nose during a cold [N3-F3]. The evidence further notes that antihistamines may cause drowsiness, dry mouth, dizziness, and other side effects, and that some antihistamines may not work well to treat the common cold [N3-F3]. That means people should not rely on antihistamines as a daily fix and should use them only cautiously.

Fifth, red flags that suggest a more serious problem are clearly spelled out in the evidence. MedlinePlus says to see a provider immediately if it becomes hard to breathe [N1-F1]. Mayo Clinic’s symptom-monitoring guidance says to call a doctor if symptoms worsen, do not improve after 10 days, or if difficulty breathing occurs [N2-F2]. WebMD also says to contact a doctor if you have trouble breathing, chest pain, a fever that doesn’t get better, can’t keep anything down, or a cough that lasts more than 2–3 weeks [N2-F2]. These are the main red flags that indicate when self-care is no longer sufficient and when medical care is needed.

In summary, the daily things to avoid or be cautious about are:
1. Avoid alcohol and tobacco smoke [N1-F1][N4-R4].
2. Avoid overusing or misusing OTC medicines, especially multi-symptom products [N1-F1][N5-F4].
3. Do not give OTC cough and cold medicine to children under age 4, and be cautious for children ages 4–6 [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2].
4. Stop nasal decongestants if they are nasal sprays after 3–4 days [N3-F3].
5. Avoid antihistamines as a routine daily fix because they are not very effective for the common cold and can have side effects [N3-F3].
6. Watch for red flags such as difficulty breathing, worsening symptoms, fever that doesn’t go away, inability to keep fluids down, or a cough lasting more than 2–3 weeks [N1-F1][N2-F2].

These cautions are all supported by the evidence and should guide daily behavior.

When to seek care and how to decide

The evidence supports a practical distinction between viral symptoms and bacterial symptoms, but it is limited in the provided excerpts. The strongest guidance is that most colds are viral, do not require specific treatment, and will resolve on their own [N1-R3][N1-F1][N4-R3]. WebMD notes that cold and flu symptoms are part of the game and that most do not require a doctor’s care, but it also says that certain symptoms are a sign to seek care [N2-R2][N2-F2]. The evidence does not provide strong direct evidence on bacterial symptoms, so the safest interpretation is that the guidance focuses on symptoms that suggest complications rather than on proving whether the infection is viral or bacterial [N2-F2].

When to see a doctor versus when to rest is clearly tied to symptom severity and duration. MedlinePlus says that if symptoms get worse or do not improve after 10 days, contact a provider [N1-F1]. It also says to see a provider immediately if it becomes hard to breathe [N1-F1]. Mayo Clinic and WebMD provide additional red flags: trouble breathing, chest pain, fever that doesn’t get better, inability to keep fluids down, and a cough lasting more than 2–3 weeks [N2-F2][N4-F2]. The evidence also says that persistent cough can be due to postnasal drip, asthma, or GERD, and that a lasting, severe cough may be whooping cough [N2-F2]. That means the decision to rest at home versus seek care depends on whether symptoms are improving, staying the same, or getting worse, and whether they are interfering with breathing or daily function.

How to describe symptoms to a provider is strongly implied in the evidence. The guidance repeatedly emphasizes specific symptoms: runny nose, cough, sore throat, fever, difficulty breathing, chest pain, trouble swallowing, inability to keep fluids down, and cough duration [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F2]. The evidence also explicitly asks the patient to describe symptoms and to note whether they are getting worse or not improving after 10 days [N1-F1][N2-F2]. This means the most useful way to describe symptoms is to give a clear account of what is present, how long it has lasted, and whether it is worsening. For example, a patient should mention whether the cough is dry or productive, whether there is yellow/green mucus, whether they can breathe easily, and whether they can keep fluids down [N1-F1][N2-F2].

The evidence also provides a practical decision framework. If symptoms are mild and improving, stay home and manage them with rest, fluids, and symptom-specific remedies [N1-F1][N4-R3]. If symptoms are worsening, persisting for more than 10 days, or accompanied by red flags like difficulty breathing, fever that doesn’t improve, or inability to keep fluids down, seek care [N1-F1][N2-F2]. The evidence does not provide a simple viral/bacterial distinction, so the safest advice is to treat the decision as: when symptoms are clearly beyond what self-care can handle, see a provider [N2-F2][N1-F1].

Overall, the evidence supports the following guidance:
1. Most colds are viral and do not require specific treatment [N1-R3][N1-F1].
2. Seek care if symptoms worsen, do not improve after 10 days, or if difficulty breathing occurs [N1-F1][N2-F2].
3. See a provider if there is trouble breathing, chest pain, fever that doesn’t go away, inability to keep fluids down, or a cough lasting more than 2–3 weeks [N2-F2].
4. Describe symptoms clearly, including what is present, how long it has lasted, and whether it is improving or getting worse [N1-F1][N2-F2].

Which over-the-counter medicines are safe and which are not

The evidence supports a cautious, evidence-based approach to choosing OTC medicines for mild symptoms. For mild symptoms, the safest OTC products are acetaminophen (Tylenol), ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), and the symptom-specific remedies that are used as needed [N1-F1][N5-F4]. MedlinePlus says acetaminophen and ibuprofen help lower fever and relieve muscle aches, while aspirin is best avoided because of the risk of stomach bleeding and Reye syndrome in children and teens [N1-F1]. Mayo Clinic similarly recommends OTC pain relievers like Tylenol, Motrin, or Advil, and it notes that honey may help coughs in adults and children over age 1 [N5-F4]. That means acetaminophen and ibuprofen are supported for mild fever and pain, while aspirin is not recommended without caution [N1-F1][N5-F4].

For symptom-specific products, the evidence supports nasal decongestants and saline nasal drops/sprays, but only with caution. MedlinePlus says nasal decongestants can help relieve stuffiness and a runny nose [N1-F1], and Mayo Clinic recommends saline nasal drops and sprays without a prescription for stuffiness [N4-R3][N5-F4]. However, the evidence also says decongestants are not a cure and should not be used for more than 3–4 days if they are nasal sprays [N3-F3]. That means nasal decongestants are safe for short-term use, but should not be used as a daily fix or beyond the recommended duration.

Antihistamines are supported only with caution and not as a routine first-line treatment. WebMD says antihistamines can help with nasal congestion and runny nose, but the evidence also says that antihistamines are not very effective for the common cold and that histamine is not the major cause of a runny nose during a cold [N3-F3]. The evidence also lists common side effects such as drowsiness, dry mouth, dizziness, low blood pressure, and others [N3-F3]. So antihistamines are not recommended as a daily routine treatment for a mild cold and should be used only if needed and with awareness of the side effects [N3-F3].

Cough suppressants and expectorants are supported conditionally. MedlinePlus says cough suppressants can help if the cough keeps you from resting or sleeping, and expectorants can help if coughing up thick mucus [N1-F1]. Mayo Clinic also mentions cough medicine, but notes that cough suppressants should be used selectively because cough is a natural defense mechanism [N4-R4]. The evidence also says that cough suppressants are for adults and older children, not for children under age 4 [N1-F1]. That means cough suppressants can be used cautiously for adults, but not routinely for children.

The evidence is very clear that some OTC products are not recommended without caution. OTC cough and cold medicine should not be used in children younger than 6 years old, and it can result in serious side effects [N6-R1][N6-R2]. Over-the-counter cough and cold medications are not effective in treating children with the common cold and might cause serious side effects, including death [N6-R3]. The evidence also says that taking too much of any medicine can be dangerous, and that some cold remedies have mixed ingredients that can cause problems if used incorrectly [N5-F4][N6-R4]. That means people should not rely on multi-symptom products without understanding the contents and should avoid giving them to children under age 4 [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2].

How to choose medicines based on symptom pattern is best summarized as “treat each symptom individually” rather than using multi-symptom products [N1-F1][N5-F4]. The evidence also says to read the labels carefully and not take too much of any one medicine [N1-F1][N5-F4]. That means choosing medicines should be guided by the main symptom: if the main problem is runny nose, nasal decongestants or saline nasal drops are the best options; if the main problem is cough, cough suppressants or expectorants are appropriate; and if the main problem is fever or pain, acetaminophen or ibuprofen are the safest choices [N1-F1][N5-F4][N3-F3].

In short, the evidence supports:
- Safe OTC products: acetaminophen, ibuprofen, saline nasal drops/sprays, nasal decongestants (short-term), cough suppressants when needed, expectorants when coughing up thick mucus, and honey for coughs in adults and children over age 1 [N1-F1][N5-F4][N3-F3].
- Not recommended without caution: aspirin, OTC cough and cold medicine in children under age 4, multi-symptom products without understanding the contents, and antihistamines as a routine treatment [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R2][N3-F3].
- How to choose: treat each symptom individually, read labels carefully, and avoid overuse or combining medicines [N1-F1][N5-F4][N6-R4].

Mayo Clinic and Mayo Clinic Health System also recommend fluids as a key part of managing cold symptoms [N4-R3][N4-R4]. This is one of the simplest and safest daily actions.

### 2. Rest and get plenty of sleep
Rest is a core part of self-care. MedlinePlus emphasizes that rest helps the body heal [N1-F1], and Mayo Clinic says rest is one of the main ways to recover [N4-R3]. Even a mild cough and runny nose can interfere with sleep, so sleep should be a priority [N4-R4].

### 3. Use saline nasal drops or sprays as needed
Saline nasal drops and sprays are supported as safe daily remedies. MedlinePlus and Mayo Clinic both recommend them for stuffiness [N1-F1][N4-R3], and Mayo Clinic Health System says they can help relieve nasal congestion [N4-R3]. These are a good first option for runny nose and nasal congestion.

### 4. Use a humidifier or cool-mist vaporizer
The evidence supports humidifiers or cool-mist vaporizers to ease breathing comfort, especially in dry air. Mayo Clinic says adjusting room humidity and temperature can help [N4-R3], while Mayo Clinic Health System and Mayo Clinic both mention humidifiers as helpful for breathing [N4-R3][N4-R2]. The evidence also notes that proper humidity can improve breathing comfort for people with allergies, asthma, or frequent cough [N4-R5].

### 5. Avoid alcohol and tobacco smoke
The evidence is clear: avoid alcohol and tobacco smoke, as they can worsen symptoms [N1-F1][N4-R4]. This is a daily caution, not just a one-time recommendation.

## 5 things you should not do every day

### 1. Use OTC cough and cold medicine in children under age 4
MedlinePlus says OTC cough and cold medicine should not be given to children younger than 4 years old, and for children ages 4–6, contact a provider before giving OTC cold medicine [N1-F1]. CDC and other sources also say OTC cold medicines are not recommended for children younger than 6 years old and can result in serious side effects [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The evidence is even stronger that over-the-counter cough and cold medications may not be effective in treating children with the common cold and may cause serious side effects [N6-R3].

### 2. Overuse or misuse OTC medicines, especially multi-symptom products
MedlinePlus warns against taking OTC medicines more than 4 times per day or for more than 2 or 3 days [N1-F1]. Mayo Clinic also says to read labels carefully and not take too much of any medicine [N5-F4]. The evidence says some cold remedies have mixed ingredients and using too much can cause serious damage [N5-F4]. So multi-symptom products should be used cautiously, if at all.

### 3. Use nasal decongestants nasal sprays for more than 3–4 days
The evidence says nasal decongestants are not a cure and should not be used for more than 3–4 days if they are nasal sprays [N3-F3]. This is an important limit on daily use, because overuse can make symptoms worse [N3-F3].

### 4. Rely on antihistamines as a routine daily fix for a mild cold
WebMD says antihistamines can help with nasal congestion and runny nose, but the evidence also says antihistamines are not very effective for the common cold and that histamine is not the major cause of a runny nose during a cold [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes common side effects such as drowsiness, dry mouth, dizziness, low blood pressure, and others [N3-F3]. So antihistamines should not be treated as a daily routine treatment.

### 5. Ignore worsening symptoms or red flags
The evidence says to seek care immediately if it becomes hard to breathe [N1-F1]. WebMD and other sources add that you should see a provider if symptoms worsen, do not improve after 10 days, or if you have trouble breathing, chest pain, fever that doesn’t get better, can’t keep anything down, or a cough lasting more than 2–3 weeks [N2-F2][N4-F2]. Even if you feel well enough to stay home, these are red flags that self-care may not be enough.

## When to seek care and how to decide
The evidence suggests that most colds are viral and do not require specific treatment [N1-R3][N1-F1]. But it also makes clear that the decision to rest at home versus seek care depends on symptom severity and duration. If symptoms worsen, do not improve after 10 days, or if difficulty breathing occurs, contact a provider [N1-F1][N2-F2]. WebMD also highlights trouble breathing, chest pain, fever that doesn’t get better, inability to keep fluids down, and cough lasting more than 2–3 weeks as reasons to seek care [N2-F2]. When you describe symptoms to a provider, be clear about what is present, how long it has lasted, and whether it is improving or getting worse [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## How to choose medicines based on symptom pattern
The evidence supports treating each symptom individually rather than using multi-symptom products [N1-F1][N5-F4]. For fever or pain, acetaminophen or ibuprofen are the safest choices [N1-F1]. For nasal congestion, saline nasal drops/sprays or nasal decongestants can be used short-term [N1-F1][N4-R3][N3-F3]. For cough, use cough suppressants only if needed and expectorants if coughing up thick mucus [N1-F1][N5-F4]. The evidence also says to read labels carefully and avoid overuse [N1-F1][N5-F4].

## Bottom line
If you have a runny nose and a mild cough without fever, the best daily routine is:

**Should do:**  
1. Drink plenty of water and other fluids without caffeine  
2. Rest and get plenty of sleep  
3. Use saline nasal drops or sprays as needed  
4. Use a humidifier or cool-mist vaporizer  
5. Avoid alcohol and tobacco smoke  

**Should not do:**  
1. Use OTC cough and cold medicine in children under age 4  
2. Overuse or misuse OTC medicines, especially multi-symptom products  
3. Use nasal decongestant nasal sprays for more than 3–4 days  
4. Rely on antihistamines as a routine daily fix for a mild cold  
5. Ignore worsening symptoms or red flags like difficulty breathing

If symptoms worsen, do not improve after 10 days, or if you develop trouble breathing, chest pain, fever that doesn’t go away, or a cough lasting more than 2–3 weeks, contact a provider [N1-F1][N2-F2].

MedlinePlus says nasal decongestants can help relieve stuffiness and a runny nose, while Mayo Clinic recommends saline nasal drops and sprays without a prescription for stuffiness [N1-F1][N4-R3][N5-F4]. Mayo Clinic also mentions cough medicine, but notes that cough suppressants should be used selectively because cough is a natural defense mechanism [N4-R4]. MedlinePlus adds that cough medicines are for adults and older children, and not for children under age 4 [N1-F1]. The broader safe daily habit is therefore to treat cough only as needed and not overuse OTC products.

Environmental and sleep habits are also central. MedlinePlus and Mayo Clinic both recommend staying away from secondhand smoke, using a humidifier or cool-mist vaporizer, and sleeping with pillows to relieve cough [N1-F1][N4-R4][N5-F4]. 1. Most colds are viral and do not require specific treatment [N1-R3][N1-F1].

# Integrated concise answer with 5 should-do and 5 should-not-do recommendations

## What the evidence says about your symptoms
The evidence is consistent that a runny nose and mild cough without fever are usually part of a viral cold or upper respiratory infection, not an emergency [N1-R3][N1-F1][N4-R3]. The main goal is symptom management at home, with rest, hydration, and symptom-specific remedies used carefully [N1-F1][N4-R3][N5-F4]. The evidence also says that most cold symptoms do not require specific treatment and that OTC medicines should be used with caution [N1-R3][N1-F1].

## 5 things you should do every day

### 1. Drink plenty of water and other fluids without caffeine
The evidence repeatedly supports hydration as a daily habit. MedlinePlus says drinking plenty of water and other fluids without caffeine helps stay hydrated, especially since coughing and blowing the nose can cause fluid loss [N1-F1]. Mayo Clinic and Mayo Clinic Health System also recommend fluids as a key part of managing cold symptoms [N4-R3][N4-R4]. This is one of the simplest and safest daily actions.

### 2. Rest and get plenty of sleep
Rest is a core part of self-care. MedlinePlus emphasizes that rest helps the body heal [N1-F1], and Mayo Clinic says rest is one of the main ways to recover [N4-R3]. Even a mild cough and runny nose can interfere with sleep, so sleep should be a priority [N4-R4].

### 3. Use saline nasal drops or sprays as needed
Saline nasal drops and sprays are supported as safe daily remedies. MedlinePlus and Mayo Clinic both recommend them for stuffiness [N1-F1][N4-R3], and Mayo Clinic Health System says they can help relieve nasal congestion [N4-R3]. These are a good first option for runny nose and nasal congestion.

### 4. Use a humidifier or cool-mist vaporizer
The evidence supports humidifiers or cool-mist vaporizers to ease breathing comfort, especially in dry air. Mayo Clinic says adjusting room humidity and temperature can help [N4-R3], while Mayo Clinic Health System and Mayo Clinic both mention humidifiers as helpful for breathing [N4-R3][N4-R2]. The evidence also notes that proper humidity can improve breathing comfort for people with allergies, asthma, or frequent cough [N4-R5].

### 5. Avoid alcohol and tobacco smoke
The evidence is clear: avoid alcohol and tobacco smoke, as they can worsen symptoms [N1-F1][N4-R4]. This is a daily caution, not just a one-time recommendation.

## 5 things you should not do every day

### 1. Use OTC cough and cold medicine in children under age 4
MedlinePlus says OTC cough and cold medicine should not be given to children younger than 4 years old, and for children ages 4–6, contact a provider before giving OTC cold medicine [N1-F1]. CDC and other sources also say OTC cold medicines are not recommended for children younger than 6 years old and can result in serious side effects [N6-R1][N6-R2]. The evidence is even stronger that over-the-counter cough and cold medications may not be effective in treating children with the common cold and may cause serious side effects [N6-R3].

### 2. Overuse or misuse OTC medicines, especially multi-symptom products
MedlinePlus warns against taking OTC medicines more than 4 times per day or for more than 2 or 3 days [N1-F1]. Mayo Clinic also says to read labels carefully and not take too much of any medicine [N5-F4]. The evidence says some cold remedies have mixed ingredients and using too much can cause serious damage [N5-F4]. So multi-symptom products should be used cautiously, if at all.

### 3. Use nasal decongestants nasal sprays for more than 3–4 days
The evidence says nasal decongestants are not a cure and should not be used for more than 3–4 days if they are nasal sprays [N3-F3]. This is an important limit on daily use, because overuse can make symptoms worse [N3-F3].

### 4. Rely on antihistamines as a routine daily fix for a mild cold
WebMD says antihistamines can help with nasal congestion and runny nose, but the evidence also says antihistamines are not very effective for the common cold and that histamine is not the major cause of a runny nose during a cold [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes common side effects such as drowsiness, dry mouth, dizziness, low blood pressure, and others [N3-F3]. So antihistamines should not be treated as a daily routine treatment.

### 5. Ignore worsening symptoms or red flags
The evidence says to seek care immediately if it becomes hard to breathe [N1-F1]. WebMD and other sources add that you should see a provider if symptoms worsen, do not improve after 10 days, or if you have trouble breathing, chest pain, fever that doesn’t get better, can’t keep anything down, or a cough lasting more than 2–3 weeks [N2-F2][N4-F2]. Even if you feel well enough to stay home, these are red flags that self-care may not be enough.

## When to seek care and how to decide
The evidence suggests that most colds are viral and do not require specific treatment [N1-R3][N1-F1]. But it also makes clear that the decision to rest at home versus seek care depends on symptom severity and duration. If symptoms worsen, do not improve after 10 days, or if difficulty breathing occurs, contact a provider [N1-F1][N2-F2]. WebMD also highlights trouble breathing, chest pain, fever that doesn’t get better, inability to keep fluids down, and cough lasting more than 2–3 weeks as reasons to seek care [N2-F2]. When you describe symptoms to a provider, be clear about what is present, how long it has lasted, and whether it is improving or getting worse [N1-F1][N2-F2].

## How to choose medicines based on symptom pattern
The evidence supports treating each symptom individually rather than using multi-symptom products [N1-F1][N5-F4]. For fever or pain, acetaminophen or ibuprofen are the safest choices [N1-F1]. For nasal congestion, saline nasal drops/sprays or nasal decongestants can be used short-term [N1-F1][N4-R3][N3-F3]. For cough, use cough suppressants only if needed and expectorants if coughing up thick mucus [N1-F1][N5-F4]. The evidence also says to read labels carefully and avoid overuse [N1-F1][N5-F4].

## Bottom line
If you have a runny nose and a mild cough without fever, the best daily routine is:

**Should do:**  
1. Drink plenty of water and other fluids without caffeine  
2. Rest and get plenty of sleep  
3. Use saline nasal drops or sprays as needed  
4. Use a humidifier or cool-mist vaporizer  
5. Avoid alcohol and tobacco smoke  

**Should not do:**  
1. Use OTC cough and cold medicine in children under age 4  
2. Overuse or misuse OTC medicines, especially multi-symptom products  
3. Use nasal decongestant nasal sprays for more than 3–4 days  
4. Rely on antihistamines as a routine daily fix for a mild cold  
5. Ignore worsening symptoms or red flags like difficulty breathing

If symptoms worsen, do not improve after 10 days, or if you develop trouble breathing, chest pain, fever that doesn’t go away, or a cough lasting more than 2–3 weeks, contact a provider [N1-F1][N2-F2].
